q-76584.name: Question 1
q-76584.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{3}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
q-76584.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}-{(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =3({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{3})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{3})}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot \sqrt{3}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-76584.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫C(x2−y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=3 for 0≤θ≤π4?

a
 2∫0π/4cos⁡θdθ
b
 33∫0π/4cos⁡2θdθ
c
6∫0π/4cos2⁡θdθ
d
 23∫0π/4sin2⁡θdθ
e
 32∫0π/4sin⁡2θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=3cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=3sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=3cos⁡θ and y=3sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π4.

Now, if f(x,y)=x2−y2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(3cos⁡θ)2−(3sin⁡θ)2=3cos2⁡θ−3sin2⁡θ=3(cos2⁡θ−sin2⁡θ)=3cos⁡2θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(3)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(3)2+02=3.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫C(x2−y2)ds=∫0π/4f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/43cos⁡2θ⋅3⋅dθ=33∫0π/4cos⁡2θdθ.

q-76609.name: Question 2
q-76609.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}xy(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=1\,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{8}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
q-76609.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{8}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=xy(1-{x}^{2})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot (1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /8}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /8}^{\pi /4}{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /8}^{\pi /4}{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-76609.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cxy(1−x2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=1 for −π8≤θ≤π4?

a
2∫−π/8π/4cos2⁡θsin⁡θdθ
b
∫−π/8π/4sin2⁡θcos⁡θdθ
c
∫−π/8π/4sin2⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
d
∫−π/8π/4cos3⁡θsin⁡θdθ
e
∫−π/8π/4sin3⁡θcos⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=1⋅cos⁡θ=cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=1⋅sin⁡θ=sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos⁡θ and y=sin⁡θ, where −π8≤θ≤π4.

Now, if f(x,y)=xy(1−x2), we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=cos⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ⋅(1−cos2⁡θ)=cos⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ⋅sin2⁡θ=sin3⁡θcos⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(1)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(1)2+02=1+0=1.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cxy(1−x2)ds=∫−π/8π/4f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/8π/4sin3⁡θcos⁡θ⋅1⋅dθ=∫−π/8π/4sin3⁡θcos⁡θdθ.

q-76607.name: Question 3
q-76607.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
q-76607.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$

q-76607.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cxyds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2cos⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
8∫0π/2cos3⁡θsin⁡θdθ
b
4∫0π/2sin⁡2θdθ
c
4∫0π/2sin2⁡θcos⁡θdθ
d
4∫0π/2cos2⁡θsin⁡θdθ
e
8∫0π/2cos⁡2θsin⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=2cos2⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2cos⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2cos2⁡θ and y=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π2.

Now, if f(x,y)=xy, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=2cos2⁡θ⋅2sin⁡θcos⁡θ=4cos3⁡θsin⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2cos⁡θ)=−2sin⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2cos⁡θ)2+(−2sin⁡θ)2=4(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=4=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cxyds=∫0π/2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/24cos3⁡θsin⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=8∫0π/2cos3⁡θsin⁡θdθ.

q-76582.name: Question 4
q-76582.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
q-76582.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-76582.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫C(x+y)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
∫0π/2sin⁡θ(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)dθ
b
2∫0π/2cos⁡θ(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)dθ
c
∫0πcos⁡θ(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)dθ
d
2∫0π/2(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)dθ
e
∫0π(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=sin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=sin⁡θcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=sin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=sin2⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=sin⁡θcos⁡θ and y=sin2⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π2.

Now, if f(x,y)=x+y, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=sin⁡θcos⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=sin⁡θ(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ).

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(sin⁡θ)=cos⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(sin⁡θ)2+(cos⁡θ)2=1=1.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫C(x+y)ds=∫0π/2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/2sin⁡θ(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)⋅1⋅dθ=∫0π/2sin⁡θ(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)dθ.

q-76611.name: Question 5
q-76611.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}(x+y)^{2}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ?$
q-76611.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x={cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)=(x+y)^{2}$, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ))}^{2} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-76611.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫C(x+y)2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=cos⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π?

a
∫0πsin⁡θ(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ)2dθ
b
∫0πcos⁡θ(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ)2dθ
c
 ∫0πcos2⁡θ(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)2dθ
d
∫0πsin2⁡θ(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ)2dθ
e
∫0πsin3⁡θ(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)2dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=cos⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos2⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=cos⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos2⁡θ and y=cos⁡θsin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π.

Now, if f(x,y)=(x+y)2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(cos2⁡θ+cos⁡θsin⁡θ)2=(cos⁡θ(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ))2=cos2⁡θ(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)2.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(cos⁡θ)=−sin⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(cos⁡θ)2+(−sin⁡θ)2=cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=1=1.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫C(x+y)2ds=∫0πf(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0πcos2⁡θ(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)2⋅1⋅dθ=∫0πcos2⁡θ(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)2dθ.

q-76685.name: Question 6
q-76685.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
q-76685.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }$, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x-y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta } \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$

$$

   

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-(0+1) \\  & =\sqrt{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

q-165415.name: Question 7
q-165415.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }\,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
q-165415.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }$, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta })^{2} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta ) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }}\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta })^{2}+{(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{4}⁡3\theta }}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{4}⁡3\theta }}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\theta +\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{1}{2}-(-\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{2+\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

q-76673.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}$ along the polar curve $r=1$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
q-76673.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

q-76353.name: Question 9
q-76353.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$
q-76353.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ){|}_{-\pi /4}^{0} \\  & =4([0-1]-[-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}]) \\  & =4(\sqrt{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

q-165416.name: Question 10
q-165416.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }\,$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{4}.$
q-165416.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }$, where $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta })^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }}\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta })^{2}+{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{4}⁡3\theta }}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{4}⁡3\theta }}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{3\pi }{4}-\frac{(-1)}{2}-(\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{2+\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

q-76768.name: Question 11
q-76768.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}\sqrt{x}y\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
q-76768.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta |\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta |=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ because $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}⟹\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \ge 0.$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\sqrt{x}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}8{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 4\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}32{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =32{\int }_{1}^{0}-{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =32{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =32\cdot \frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}({1}^{3}-{0}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-76339.name: Question 12
q-76339.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
q-76339.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =5{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=5{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 5{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =25{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}25{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 5\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =125{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}125{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =125{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =125\cdot \frac{1}{4}{u}^{4}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{125}{4}({1}^{4}-{0}^{4}) \\  & =\frac{125}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =27{sin}^{5}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{3}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{u}^{3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}({(\frac{1}{2})}^{5/2}-{0}^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{5}}} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$
